name: Achan
title: The Man Who Stole from the Devoted Things at Jericho
summary: Achan, son of Karmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, from the tribe of Judah, is known for taking some of the devoted things (herem) after the conquest of Jericho. Despite God's clear command not to take anything that was set apart for destruction, Achan secretly took a beautiful robe from Shinar, along with silver and a bar of gold, and hid them under his tent. His sin led to Israel's unexpected defeat at Ai and revealed a serious breach of covenant among the people. When Achan was identified by casting lots, he confessed his wrongdoing. He was brought to the Valley of Achor together with his family, his livestock, and all that he owned, where judgment was carried out by stoning. The story is a powerful testimony to how one person's disobedience and greed can affect the entire community, and it underscores the grave seriousness of breaking covenant with God. At the same time, the prophet Hosea points forward to a day when the Valley of Achor—the "Valley of Trouble"—will be transformed into a door of hope.
roles: Israelite man from the tribe of Judah
Participant in the conquest of Canaan

keyEvents.title: The Conquest of Jericho and the Devoted Things
keyEvents.description: After Israel conquered Jericho, Achan secretly took a beautiful robe from Shinar, 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels from the devoted things, despite God's clear command not to take anything that was set apart for destruction.

keyEvents.title: Israel's Defeat at Ai
keyEvents.description: Because of Achan's sin, Israel was defeated by the men of Ai, and about 36 Israelites fell. The defeat shocked Joshua and the people, revealing that something was seriously wrong in Israel's relationship with God.

keyEvents.title: Joshua's Prayer and God's Answer
keyEvents.description: Joshua fell on his face before the ark of the Lord and lamented the defeat. God revealed that someone in Israel had taken from the devoted things, broken the covenant, and lied. The sin had to be removed before Israel could stand against its enemies.

keyEvents.title: Achan Will Be Exposed by Casting Lots
keyEvents.description: God commanded that the tribes be presented, and by casting lots, first the tribe of Judah was selected, then Zerah's clan, next Achar's family, further Carmi's household, and finally Achan was pointed out as the guilty one.

keyEvents.title: Achan's Confession
keyEvents.description: At Joshua's urging to give glory to the Lord, the God of Israel, Achan confessed that he had seen a beautiful robe from Shinar, 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels. He coveted them, took them, and hid them in the ground beneath his tent.

keyEvents.title: The Judgment on Achan in the Valley of Achor
keyEvents.description: Achan was brought to the Valley of Achor along with the stolen goods, his sons and daughters, his livestock, and all that he owned. All Israel stoned him and burned them with fire, and they raised a large pile of stones over him. The place was called the Valley of Achor, which means 'Valley of Trouble'.

versions.summary: Achan, son of Carmi, from the tribe of Judah, is known for taking some of the devoted things after the conquest of Jericho. His sin led to Israel's defeat at Ai and brought judgment upon himself and his family. He stands as a warning example of how one person's disobedience can affect the entire community.
versions.title: The Man Who Stole from the Devoted Things
versions.reason: [minor] The title is good and descriptive but could be slightly refined. "The devoted thing" is correct terminology (herem), but one might consider mentioning Jericho for context.; [major] Achan's lineage is more detailed in Joshua 7:1 and 7:18. He is the son of Karmi, son of Zabdi (Zimri in 1 Chron 2:6), son of Zerah, from the tribe of Judah. Although we only have "father" as a field, we should ensure the genealogy is correctly mentioned in the summary.; [major] In Joshua 7:17–18, "Zabdi's family" is mentioned, but it is Karmi's household that is singled out, and then Achan. The description says "Zabdi's family and finally Achan," but the link with Karmi's household is missing. The order is: tribe of Judah → Zerah's clan → Zabdi's house → Karmi's house → Achan.; [minor] Achan is not explicitly called a "warrior" in the text, although he participated in the military operation. He was an Israelite man from the tribe of Judah. One might consider adding "Israelite" or adjusting the role.; [major] Footnotes are missing that cover important historical, linguistic, and theological aspects of the Achan story—for example, the concept of "herem" (devotion), the meaning of the name Valley of Achor, the variant names Achan/Akar, and archaeological conditions around Jericho and Ai.

Despite God's clear command not to take anything that was set apart for destruction, Achan secretly took a beautiful robe, silver, and a bar of gold and hid them under his tent. His sin led to Israel's unexpected defeat at Ai and brought judgment upon himself and his entire family in the Valley of Achor. Achan serves as a warning example of how one person's disobedience and greed can affect the whole community, and the story emphasizes the seriousness of breaking covenant with God.

Although we do not know their names, the children field could contain a note, or it could be mentioned in the summary that he had children. The current children array is empty, but this is acceptable since the names are unknown.; [minor] The role 'warrior' is reasonably assumed given the context (the conquest of Jericho), but the Bible does not explicitly call him a warrior. An additional footnote could address the historical context for the destruction of Jericho and archaeological findings related to this, but the existing footnotes are already comprehensive.

footnotes.text: The name Achan (עָכָן) varies in biblical sources. In 1 Chronicles 2:7 he is called Akar (עָכָר), which means 'the bringer of trouble' – a wordplay on the Valley of Achor (עָכוֹר). It is possible that 'Akar' is a deliberate alteration of the name to emphasize his role as a bringer of trouble for Israel.

The term 'herem' (חֵרֶם), often translated as 'devoted thing' or 'the devoted', means that war spoils were dedicated to God and could not be taken by individuals. In ancient Near Eastern warfare, it was common for conquered goods to be dedicated to the gods. Violating the herem was considered sacrilege and theft from God Himself.

The Valley of Achor (עֵמֶק עָכוֹר) has been identified with the Buqe'ah valley or el-Buqei'a west of Qumran. The prophet Hosea (Hos 2:17) prophesies that the Valley of Achor will one day become 'a door of hope', giving the place a future dimension of redemption in biblical theology.

The collective punishment of Achan's family raises important theological questions. In ancient Israelite thought, the family was a solidary unit, and the sin of the head of household affected the entire household. This reflects a corporate understanding of guilt that was widespread in the ancient Near East but later nuanced, for example, in Ezekiel 18.

The rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Sanhedrin 44a) discusses Achan's case in detail. Some rabbis claimed that Achan had committed several sins earlier, while others emphasized his sincere confession as an example of repentance (teshuva). Joshua's exhortation 'Give glory to the Lord, the God of Israel' (Josh 7:19) became a model for confession formulas in rabbinic tradition.

The cloak from Shinar (שִׁנְעָר) that Achan took points back to the Babylonian region (Gen 10:10; 11:2). The fact that such a luxury item existed in Jericho testifies to widespread trade networks in the late Bronze Age between Mesopotamia and Canaan. The Shinar cloak may have been an embroidered, high-status garment of the type known from Mesopotamian iconographic sources.
